cards.meaning: JavaScript objects form a prototype chain. When you read a property that is not an own property, the engine walks that object's internal [[Prototype]] link, then that object's prototype, and so on, until it finds the property or reaches null. There is no separate class-instance runtime underneath ES6 class.
Every ordinary object has an internal slot [[Prototype]]: either another object or null. That link is how lookup and inheritance walk the chain.

cards.front: How should you read an object's [[Prototype]]?
cards.meaning: Prefer Object.getPrototypeOf(obj). __proto__ is a legacy accessor on Object.prototype — avoid it in new code, but recognize it in interviews and debugging.
A plain object literal's [[Prototype]] is Object.prototype. Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype) === null — that is the end of the chain.

cards.front: Property miss on obj — what happens?
cards.meaning: Walk [[Prototype]] link: check own properties, then prototype object, repeat until null → undefined for ordinary gets. Assignment usually creates own property on obj (shadowing), not mutating prototype.

cards.front: After obj.kind = 'dog', delete obj.kind — what does obj.kind read?
cards.meaning: The own property is gone, so lookup walks the chain again and finds proto.kind. Shadowing hid the prototype value; delete reveals it.
Shared behavior without copying methods onto every object. One speak function on Animal.prototype serves all instances; each instance only stores its own data (name, etc.).
Most objects ultimately delegate to Object.prototype, which holds widely used methods: toString, hasOwnProperty (legacy style), valueOf, and similar.
Dictionary with no inherited Object.prototype junk — no inherited toString/hasOwnProperty on the chain.
cards.example: dict.toString // undefined — useful for safe key maps

cards.meaning: A new object whose [[Prototype]] is proto (or null). Property gets that miss on the new object delegate to proto.
cards.example: const dog = Object.create(animal); dog.speak(); // 'sound'; Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal

cards.meaning: Optional second argument can define own properties via property descriptors. Less common in interviews; know it exists.

cards.front: Draw the usual instance prototype chain?
cards.meaning: instance → Animal.prototype → Object.prototype → null. That is the mental model for where shared methods and Object.prototype methods are found.

cards.front: Constructor pattern: own data vs shared methods?
cards.meaning: Own properties are set in the constructor on this (per instance). Shared methods are assigned on Constructor.prototype — one function for all instances.
cards.example: function Animal(name) { this.name = name; } Animal.prototype.speak = function () { return this.name + ' makes a sound'; }

cards.meaning: Create empty object; set its [[Prototype]] to Ctor.prototype; call Ctor with this = new object; return new object unless constructor returns another object (primitives ignored).
That object replaces the default new instance as the result of new. Returning a primitive is ignored; instance with own fields remains.
cards.example: function Weird() { this.a = 1; return { b: 2 }; } new Weird(); // { b: 2 }

cards.front: Constructor returns 5 — what is new Normal()?
cards.meaning: A returned primitive is ignored. The result is the new instance with own fields from this.
cards.example: function Normal() { this.a = 1; return 5; } new Normal(); // { a: 1 }

cards.meaning: Animal.prototype is the object instances link to via new. getPrototypeOf(dog) is dog's actual [[Prototype]] (usually Animal.prototype). dog.prototype is usually undefined — instances aren't constructors.
Animal.prototype.constructor === Animal is true by default (a convention). After replacing Dog.prototype with Object.create(...), you repair constructor back to Dog.

cards.front: Call a constructor as a plain function (no new)?
cards.meaning: Uses default this binding: in strict mode this.name = ... throws; in sloppy mode it can create or pollute globals. Prefer class (throws without new) or always invoke with new.

cards.front: What does obj instanceof Ctor check?
cards.meaning: Whether Ctor.prototype appears anywhere on obj's prototype chain — not exclusive construction history. Cross-realm and manual setPrototypeOf can surprise.
cards.example: dog instanceof Animal; // true  dog instanceof Object; // true  dog instanceof Array; // false

cards.meaning: Manual Object.setPrototypeOf / Object.create, cross-realm objects (iframe/another window has a different Array.prototype), and rare Symbol.hasInstance customization. It is not a perfect exclusive type check.

cards.front: Own vs inherited: hasOwnProperty, Object.hasOwn, in?
cards.meaning: hasOwnProperty/Object.hasOwn are true for own data (name) and false for prototype methods (speak). Object.hasOwn is the modern preferred own check. The in operator sees inherited properties too: 'speak' in dog → true.

ES6 class is syntax over constructor + prototype with real differences: strict body, TDZ until class line, TypeError without new, non-enumerable prototype methods. Still: methods on Ctor.prototype, own data from constructor/fields.
Always strict. A classic function constructor is strict only if requested. That is one real difference, not just prettier syntax.
ReferenceError — class declarations are TDZ'd like let, unlike hoisted function constructors.
cards.example: const x = new Person(); class Person {} // ReferenceError

cards.front: Call class A as A() without new?
cards.meaning: TypeError: Class constructor A cannot be invoked without 'new'. Classic function constructors instead get silent wrong this / pollution risk.

cards.front: Are class-body methods enumerable on the prototype?
cards.meaning: No — methods in a class body are non-enumerable on the prototype. Manual Constructor.prototype.foo = ... is enumerable by default.

cards.front: Class field count = 0 vs method inc() — where stored?
cards.meaning: count is an own property per instance (set like constructor init). inc lives on Counter.prototype — one shared function.
a.inc === b.inc is true (same function on the prototype). a.count and b.count start equal numerically but are different own properties; after a.count = 5, b.count is still 0.
cards.example: const a = new Counter(); const b = new Counter(); a.count = 5; b.count; // 0

cards.front: Prototype method vs arrow class field?
cards.meaning: Method on Ctor.prototype — one shared function, this from call site. Arrow instance field — own property per instance, lexical this to instance at construction; costs extra allocation per instance, stable detached callbacks.
cards.notes: Avoids manual .bind() for older React class event handlers.

cards.meaning: Dog.prototype's [[Prototype]] is Animal.prototype; Dog's [[Prototype]] is Animal (statics). super() in subclass constructor runs parent constructor before using this. super.method() uses parent prototype chain.

cards.front: Subclass constructor: use this before super()?
cards.meaning: Invalid — must call super() before accessing this in a derived class constructor.
d.speak() is 'Rex noise (woof)' — subclass speak uses super.speak() then appends. d instanceof Dog and d instanceof Animal are both true because both prototypes appear on the chain.
cards.example: class Dog extends Animal { constructor(name, breed) { super(name); this.breed = breed; } speak() { return `${super.speak()} (woof)`; } }

cards.meaning: getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype) === Animal.prototype (instance method chain). getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal (static inheritance — constructors inherit too).
The method on the parent prototype chain — not a dynamic “caller” lookup. super() in the constructor invokes the parent constructor for instance initialization.

cards.front: Pre-class: Animal.call(this, name) is like what?
cards.meaning: Like super() for instance data: run the parent constructor against the child instance so own fields are initialized, then wire prototypes separately with Object.create.
Object.create(Animal.prototype), then repair Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog. Wrong: Dog.prototype = Animal.prototype (shared one object, methods overwrite each other).

setPrototypeOf can mutate an existing object's [[Prototype]]; prefer Object.create when building the link for a new prototype object. Mutating prototypes of live objects is slower and surprising — know it, don't casually use it.

cards.front: Where do class static members live?
cards.meaning: On the constructor function itself (called as User.createGuest(), not on an instance), and they follow the constructor's prototype chain with extends — not on instances.
cards.example: class User { static createGuest() { return new User('guest'); } } User.createGuest();

cards.front: When do Nest/TS decorators attach DI metadata?
cards.meaning: Decorators are functions that run at class definition time and can attach metadata (Reflect.metadata). TypeScript can emit design-time type metadata for constructor parameters so the DI container knows what to inject.

cards.front: Nest DI and classes — one sentence?
cards.meaning: Providers are constructors; DI reads metadata emitted on the class (e.g. constructor param types) to know what to inject — classes are runtime values; prototype methods are shared instance behavior.
It changes behavior for all instances that still delegate to that prototype — powerful and dangerous. Shared methods are not copies on each instance unless you install arrows/fields per instance.

cards.front: Prototypes vs this — what question does each answer?
cards.meaning: Prototypes answer where the function is found; this answers which receiver was used when calling it. this inside prototype methods still follows call-site rules.
